accuracy.evidence: Follows Robinson's SQ3R (1946) for the survey and question stages, and the English curriculum aims of retrieving and recording information from non-fiction (KS2) and reading for a range of purposes (KS3). The study-strategy claims match Dunlosky et al. (2013): practice testing rated high in usefulness, while rereading and highlighting are rated low. The bee facts were checked: a queen lays up to about 2,000 eggs a day, the waggle run's direction gives the bearing and its length gives the distance, and one worker makes about 1/12 teaspoon of honey.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets reading every page word by word (the 'Read every word' button shows the full word cost), using skimming for detail and scanning for gist (Challenge items and mastery m3), yes or no questions from headings (step 2 traps and m5), and the illusion that rereading or highlighting is learning (step 4 prediction, the Peek warning and m6). The waggle-direction sentence is a near-miss trap in step 3, because it answers which way and not how far.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagskim draws a paper fact sheet whose words are grey bars that a reading mode reveals: headings and first lines for skimming, a lens line with digits showing for scanning, a question under each heading, a single section for close reading, and a cover sheet for recall. It passes the 30% shingle gate and is unlike the gist, note-taking and text-structure labs, which sort cards or highlight given text.

lab_teaches.evidence: One page carries all five moves in SQ3R order, so the child sees how each strategy shows a different slice of the same text. Skim shows 46 of 128 words and gives the map, scan shows only the digits, questions turn headings into goals, close reading finds the one sentence that answers, and recall is done with the page covered. The Challenge then asks which strategy fits a new job.

predictions.evidence: Four steps ask for a prediction before acting: the best first move with two minutes, what your eyes hunt for, why to make questions, and what helps memory a week later. The choice is locked, and the result quotes it back with a spot-on line, or the reveal explains the gap, for example that highlighting is rated low.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six Challenge questions mix strategy choice (the year a war ended means scan, a chapter's topic means skim, explaining honey means reading closely), heading questions, highlighting and scanning for names. Each wrong answer has its own why() reply, such as 'Skimming gives the big picture. For one fact, like a year, scan for the digits.' A rule card above the questions sums up the four moves.

readability.evidence: The learner text is at about Flesch-Kincaid grade 2.9 and the adult notes at 7.4. Both use the exact terms skim, scan, close reading, heading, gist and SQ3R, each defined in plain words. Every lab step has three short sentences, and each task opens with a verb.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph does a distinct job. The learner text covers choosing by purpose, skimming, scanning, and questions plus recall. The adult notes cover the source and curriculum link, the difference between skimming and scanning, named mistakes with the Dunlosky ratings, and what the lab does. The family tip is a concrete two-minute routine, and the content gate's similarity is under 12%.

mobile.evidence: Checked at phone width in iPhone dark and Android light. The sheet uses a taller canvas on narrow screens and shrinks its type step by step until all four sections fit, with nothing cut off and no sideways scrolling. Text wraps to the canvas width, and each sentence is its own tap target. Every action has a full-width wrap button at least 44 px tall (Lens up, Lens down, Sentence 1 to 3, and the answer choices).

accessibility.evidence: The canvas has an aria-label that mirrors the live caption, for example 'Found it: up to 2,000 eggs a day'. Every tap or swipe has a button twin with a descriptive aria-label such as 'Choose: The longer the waggle...'. The sheet is always dark ink on paper, so contrast holds in both themes, the reveal state is described in words, and sound is off by default.

sources: Robinson, F. P. (1946) Effective Study. Harper & Brothers (SQ3R: survey, question, read, recite, review)

Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J. & Willingham, D. T. (2013) Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques, Psychological Science in the Public Interest 14(1): 4-58
Department for Education (2013/2014) National curriculum in England: English programmes of study, KS2 Years 5-6 reading comprehension and KS3 reading
von Frisch, K. (1967) The Dance Language and Orientation of Bees (waggle run direction and duration)
